title: Iron studies
subtitle: Serum iron, ferritin, transferrin saturation and TIBC for iron status assessment
summary: Iron profile measurement for assessment of iron deficiency, iron overload, and anaemia diagnosis.
introduction: Iron studies include serum iron, ferritin, transferrin saturation (TSAT), and total iron-binding capacity (TIBC). Ferritin is the most commonly used marker of iron stores. Used in combination with FBC to diagnose iron deficiency anaemia and assess iron overload.

rows.name: Serum ferritin
lowInterpretation: Ferritin <15 ng/mL: iron deficiency (depleted iron stores). Confirms diagnosis if MCV is low (microcytic anaemia).
Ferritin 15–30 ng/mL: iron-depleted but not yet anaemic; risk of developing anaemia if losses continue.
highInterpretation: Ferritin >200 ng/mL (female) or >300 ng/mL (male): iron overload or secondary elevation.
Primary iron overload: hereditary haemochromatosis (elevated TSAT >45%), secondary to transfusions or haemolysis.
Secondary elevation (common): acute inflammation/infection, liver disease, malignancy, renal failure. Ferritin is acute-phase reactant; always check CRP.
notes: Ferritin is non-specific (elevated in inflammation, infection, malignancy, cirrhosis).
In anaemia of chronic disease: ferritin often normal-to-elevated despite iron deficiency; use TSAT (<20%) to confirm iron deficiency.
Optimal threshold varies by age, sex, and lab; use lab-specific ranges.

rows.name: Transferrin saturation (TSAT)
lowInterpretation: TSAT <20%: iron deficiency (cannot saturate transferrin when iron depleted). Specific for iron deficiency in anaemia of chronic disease.
TSAT 20–30%: normal or mildly reduced; may indicate mild iron deficiency or resolving iron stores.
highInterpretation: TSAT >55%: highly specific for hereditary haemochromatosis (combined with ferritin >200 ng/mL).
notes: More specific for iron deficiency than ferritin; useful to confirm iron deficiency in inflammatory anaemia.
TSAT <20% supports iron deficiency even if ferritin is normal-to-high (as in chronic inflammation).

urgentFindings: Ferritin <15 ng/mL + MCV <80 fL + Hb <110 g/L (female): iron deficiency anaemia confirmed; investigate source (GI bleeding, menorrhagia).
TSAT >45% + ferritin >200 ng/mL + elevated transaminases: suspect haemochromatosis; refer for HFE genotyping and liver assessment.
Ferritin >500 ng/mL + fever + elevated inflammatory markers: acute phase response; repeat after infection resolves to assess true iron status.
overrides: Never diagnose iron deficiency on ferritin alone if inflammation present; use TSAT <20% as supporting evidence.
Iron replacement therapy only after confirming iron deficiency AND identifying/addressing source of loss.
Elevated ferritin does not always mean iron overload; always check CRP and consider alternative diagnoses.

commonPatterns.title: Iron deficiency anaemia
interpretation: Likely source: GI bleeding or menorrhagia
actions: Identify source of iron loss (GI investigations, menstrual history)
Iron supplementation or transfusion if severe
Repeat iron studies after source control

commonPatterns.title: Anaemia of chronic disease
interpretation: Iron deficiency coexists with chronic inflammation
Ferritin elevated from acute phase, not iron stores
Requires both iron and inflammation management
actions: Treat underlying chronic disease (infection, autoimmune, cancer)
Consider iron supplementation once inflammation controlled
Address iron loss source if present

commonPatterns.title: Hereditary haemochromatosis
interpretation: Risk of liver cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma
actions: Liver ultrasound and assessment for cirrhosis

furtherTesting.test: GI bleeding source investigation (if iron deficiency)
rationale: Occult blood test, endoscopy if age >50 or alarm features
Screen for menorrhagia, coeliac serology, parasites
Assess for cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma risk
